quote: metabolic derangements, and — always — hypoglycemia, hypoxia, and intracranial catastrophe as can't-miss items.
problem: The can't-miss list for delirium in a febrile older adult omits alcohol/sedative-hypnotic withdrawal and CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis); nowhere does the page prompt a substance-use history, although the medication list is collateral from the daughter only.
whyItMatters: The page's central pharmacologic rule (avoid benzodiazepines, give an antipsychotic) is reversed in withdrawal; a student who never asks about alcohol or benzodiazepine use could endorse haloperidol for unrecognized withdrawal delirium (lowered seizure threshold, untreated DTs), and fever plus delirium without CNS infection on the list invites anchoring on the UTI.
evidence: Wilson MP et al., Project BETA psychopharmacology workgroup, West J Emerg Med 2012 (benzodiazepines first-line for alcohol/sedative withdrawal); APA Practice Guideline for Delirium (1999) / NICE CG103 — assess for withdrawal and CNS infection as precipitants; the page's own Q5 depends on recognizing the withdrawal exception.
correction: metabolic derangements, and — always — hypoglycemia, hypoxia, alcohol or sedative (benzodiazepine) withdrawal (ask the daughter directly about drinking and sleeping pills), CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis — fever plus confusion), and intracranial catastrophe as can't-miss items.

quote: *Teaching point:* Verbal de-escalation before medication, and medication before physical restraint.
problem: Asked what an MS3 does 'first' when a patient is swinging at staff, the answer begins with verbal de-escalation and omits the student's actual first moves: keep a safe distance and exit, call for help, and act under the supervising clinician/team lead.
whyItMatters: A student may approach a combative patient alone to 'de-escalate', risking injury to themselves and escalation of the patient; students act only under supervision and should not lead the response.
evidence: Richmond JS et al., Project BETA de-escalation workgroup, West J Emerg Med 2012 — Domain 1 'respect personal space' (two arm's lengths, clear exit) and a single designated, trained lead; the chunk's own facilitator note frames content around 'escalation to security'.
correction: *Teaching point:* First, make the scene safe: step back to a safe distance with a clear exit, call for help (nurse, security, your supervising resident/attending), and let one experienced team member lead — you participate under supervision. Then: verbal de-escalation before medication, and medication before physical restraint.

quote: (The exception: sedative-hypnotic or alcohol withdrawal, where benzodiazepines are first-line.) Start low, go slow, and reassess.
problem: The page recommends haloperidol for delirium in a 74-year-old whose differential includes unrecognized dementia (and whose Q2 cites visual hallucinations/fluctuation — core DLB features) but never flags severe neuroleptic sensitivity in Lewy body dementia or Parkinson disease.
whyItMatters: Haloperidol in DLB/PD can precipitate severe rigidity, falls, NMS-like reactions and death; a student carrying 'low-dose haloperidol is preferred' into an older adult with parkinsonism would recommend the wrong agent.
evidence: McKeith IG et al., DLB Consortium 4th consensus report, Neurology 2017 (severe neuroleptic sensitivity; avoid typical antipsychotics); AGS Beers Criteria 2023 (avoid antipsychotics except quetiapine/clozapine/pimavanserin in Parkinson disease).
correction: (The exception: sedative-hypnotic or alcohol withdrawal, where benzodiazepines are first-line.) Avoid haloperidol if the patient has Parkinson disease or possible Lewy body dementia (parkinsonism, visual hallucinations, fluctuations) — severe antipsychotic sensitivity; ask your team. Start low, go slow, and reassess.

quote: benzodiazepines contraindicated in non-withdrawal delirium in the elderly
problem: 'Contraindicated' overstates the body text ('should generally be AVOIDED'); benzodiazepines remain indicated in delirium with co-occurring catatonia, seizures, or for procedural/palliative sedation.
whyItMatters: Students may believe benzodiazepines are absolutely forbidden and oppose lorazepam when catatonia or seizures coexist with delirium.
evidence: Wilson MP et al., Project BETA 2012 ('avoid' benzodiazepines in non-withdrawal delirium, not an absolute contraindication); catatonia literature (lorazepam first-line even with delirium features).
correction: benzodiazepines generally avoided in non-withdrawal delirium in the elderly (exceptions: withdrawal, catatonia, seizures)

quote: avoid olanzapine + parenteral benzodiazepine stacking in alcohol-intoxicated patients [2]
problem: The IM olanzapine + parenteral benzodiazepine caution is narrowed to alcohol-intoxicated patients; the FDA label says concomitant IM olanzapine and parenteral benzodiazepine is not recommended in general (cardiorespiratory depression, deaths reported), and the same plan offers IM olanzapine and IM midazolam as sequential options for a non-alcohol patient.
whyItMatters: A resident could give midazolam 5 mg IM then olanzapine 10 mg IM (or vice versa) to Patient B, believing the caution does not apply because he is not alcohol-intoxicated, risking hypotension/respiratory depression.
evidence: ZYPREXA IntraMuscular USPI (Warnings/Drug Interactions): concomitant IM olanzapine and parenteral benzodiazepine has not been studied and is not recommended; if considered, monitor for excessive sedation and cardiorespiratory depression. Wilson MP et al., Project BETA 2012, notes the caution is heightened with alcohol.
correction: avoid combining IM olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine (not recommended per FDA label; cardiorespiratory depression), especially in alcohol-intoxicated patients [2]
verified: WebSearch (label sources located); label text from recall

quote: 6. Hyperactive delirium of medical origin (metabolic, post-ictal).
problem: Patient B's differential omits traumatic brain injury/intracranial hemorrhage despite arrival by police after an altercation, and omits excited catatonia and serotonin toxicity (diaphoresis, mydriasis, tachycardia, agitation).
whyItMatters: Chemical sedation of an agitated patient with an unrecognized head injury masks neurologic deterioration; IM antipsychotics given for unrecognized excited catatonia can precipitate malignant catatonia/NMS; serotonin toxicity needs clonus/hyperreflexia check before dopamine antagonists.
evidence: Wilson MP et al., Project BETA 2012 and Nordstrom K et al., Project BETA medical evaluation workgroup, West J Emerg Med 2012 (head trauma among medical causes of agitation to exclude); Fink & Taylor catatonia literature; Boyer & Shannon NEJM 2005 (serotonin syndrome).
correction:
6. Hyperactive delirium of medical origin (metabolic, post-ictal).
7. Traumatic brain injury/intracranial hemorrhage — altercation with police; examine for head trauma before and after sedation.
8. Excited catatonia or serotonin toxicity — check catatonic signs and clonus/hyperreflexia before a dopamine antagonist.

quote: 6. Nonconvulsive status epilepticus — consider if fluctuation persists despite source control.
problem: Patient A's ranked differential (febrile delirium) omits alcohol/sedative-hypnotic withdrawal and CNS infection, yet the plan says flatly 'Avoid benzodiazepines'; the ED's lorazepam proposal is rejected without first excluding withdrawal.
whyItMatters: If Patient A is in unrecognized alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, the page's counter-proposal (haloperidol, no benzodiazepine) is the wrong treatment; fever with delirium also requires considering meningitis/encephalitis (LP) when the source is uncertain.
evidence: Wilson MP et al., Project BETA 2012 (withdrawal exception); ASAM Alcohol Withdrawal Management Guideline 2020; IDSA encephalitis guidance (Tunkel 2008) — evaluate for CNS infection in fever with altered mental status.
correction:
6. Nonconvulsive status epilepticus — consider if fluctuation persists despite source control.
6a. Alcohol or sedative-hypnotic withdrawal — obtain substance history/collateral before endorsing 'no benzodiazepines'; CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) — LP if source uncertain or meningismus.

quote: if IM required: droperidol 5 mg or olanzapine 10 mg IM as effective single agents [3,5]; midazolam 5 mg IM when speed is paramount and airway monitoring is available [3];
problem: For a patient with a sympathomimetic toxidrome 'high on the differential', the plan leads with antipsychotics and relegates benzodiazepines to 'when speed is paramount', contradicting Q1 (and Project BETA) which favors benzodiazepines for CNS-stimulant intoxication; Cole et al.'s droperidol/olanzapine data come from a population 86% alcohol-intoxicated.
whyItMatters: Residents may default to antipsychotic monotherapy in stimulant toxicity, forgoing the agent that also treats sympathomimetic seizures/hyperadrenergic state, and extrapolate alcohol-intoxication data to stimulant intoxication.
evidence: Wilson MP et al., Project BETA 2012: benzodiazepines are first-line for agitation from CNS-stimulant intoxication; Cole JB et al., Ann Emerg Med 2021 abstract: 86% of 1,257 patients had agitation owing to alcohol intoxication.
correction: if IM required and a sympathomimetic toxidrome is likely: a benzodiazepine first (e.g., midazolam 5 mg IM, with airway monitoring) per BETA [2,3]; droperidol 5 mg or olanzapine 10 mg IM are effective alternatives (note Cole's cohort was 86% alcohol-intoxicated) [3,5];
verified: PubMed metadata for Cole 2021 (PMID 33846015) and Klein 2018 (PMID 29885904)

quote: Post-sedation: vitals q15 min, SpO2/capnography where available, ECG when feasible, toxicologic and metabolic workup, serial reassessment;
problem: Monitoring for a restrained/sedated patient with a suspected sympathomimetic toxidrome omits temperature and CK, and nothing on the page warns about restraint-related harms (hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, positional asphyxia with prone restraint).
whyItMatters: Stimulant-intoxicated patients who struggle against restraint are at highest risk of hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis/AKI and sudden death; a resident following this list would not check core temperature or CK.
evidence: CMS 42 CFR 482.13(e) (monitoring of restrained patients); ACEP 2023 policy on hyperactive delirium with severe agitation and restraint deaths; standard toxicology references (Goldfrank) on sympathomimetic hyperthermia/rhabdomyolysis.
correction: Post-sedation: vitals q15 min including temperature, SpO2/capnography where available, ECG when feasible, CK and toxicologic/metabolic workup (hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis risk, especially if he struggled against restraint; never restrain prone), serial reassessment;

quote: For any physical restraint: time-limited orders, face-to-face evaluation, frequent reassessment, and early release criteria.
problem: The restraint-governance teaching point for residents omits the federal specifics they carry accountability for: no PRN orders, adult order limit of 4 h (renewal), face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour, continuous monitoring, and post-event debriefing; it also omits positional-asphyxia risk.
whyItMatters: Residents write and renew these orders; vague 'time-limited'/'face-to-face' leaves them unable to meet CMS Conditions of Participation that apply in every Medicare-participating hospital.
evidence: CMS Conditions of Participation, 42 CFR 482.13(e)(5)-(8),(12),(16) and 482.13(f): orders never PRN; violent/self-destructive restraint orders ≤4 h adults (2 h ages 9–17, 1 h <9), renewable up to 24 h before new face-to-face; in-person evaluation within 1 hour of initiation; documentation; state law/policy may be stricter.
correction: For any physical restraint (CMS 42 CFR 482.13; state rules may be stricter): a non-PRN, time-limited order (≤4 h for adults, renewed only after reassessment), an in-person face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour, continuous monitoring (never prone; airway, circulation, temperature), release as soon as criteria are met, and a post-event debrief.

quote: Reasonable practice: screen for known long-QT/recent QT-prolonging drug load when feasible, obtain ECG when the clinical situation allows, and avoid routine "QTc paralysis" that delays treatment of dangerous agitation.
problem: The page presents the droperidol boxed warning as historical, without stating that it remains on the current US label (pre-dose 12-lead ECG, ECG monitoring for 2–3 h after), and that agitation is an off-label use (labelled indication: nausea/vomiting from surgical/diagnostic procedures).
whyItMatters: Residents carry med-legal accountability; giving droperidol without ECG outside an institutional protocol departs from the label, and the page's framing could lead them to omit post-dose cardiac monitoring.
evidence: Droperidol injection USPI (DailyMed): boxed warning — 12-lead ECG prior to administration; ECG monitoring for 2–3 hours after; reserved for patients who fail other treatments; indication = reducing nausea/vomiting with surgical and diagnostic procedures. Mattson A et al., AJHP 2020 (review supports ED use but notes the warning persists).
correction: Reasonable practice: know that the boxed warning is still on the label (pre-dose 12-lead ECG, ECG monitoring for 2–3 h) and that agitation is an off-label use; follow an institutional ED droperidol protocol, screen for known long-QT/recent QT-prolonging drug load when feasible, obtain ECG when the clinical situation allows, monitor after dosing, and avoid routine "QTc paralysis" that delays treatment of dangerous agitation.
verified: WebSearch (DailyMed/label sources located); label content from recall

quote: haloperidol 0.5–1 mg IV/IM (or low-dose SGA), reassess q30–60 min, cumulative-dose cap and EPS/QTc vigilance [2].
problem: Haloperidol is recommended for a 74-year-old whose differential includes unrecognized major neurocognitive disorder, with no warning about Lewy body dementia/Parkinson disease antipsychotic sensitivity (and no note that IV haloperidol is off-label with its own QT caution).
whyItMatters: Haloperidol in DLB/PD can cause severe rigidity, immobility, NMS-like reactions and death; residents should screen for parkinsonism/DLB features before choosing the agent.
evidence: McKeith IG et al., DLB Consortium 4th consensus, Neurology 2017; AGS Beers Criteria 2023; FDA 2007 information for healthcare professionals on IV haloperidol (QT prolongation/TdP; not approved IV).
correction: haloperidol 0.5–1 mg IV/IM (or low-dose SGA), reassess q30–60 min, cumulative-dose cap and EPS/QTc vigilance [2] (IV haloperidol is off-label — ECG monitoring); avoid haloperidol if Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia is known or suspected — very-low-dose quetiapine if an antipsychotic is unavoidable.

quote: Meta-analysis of ED/prehospital data shows dissociative-dose ketamine (typically 4–5 mg/kg IM) achieves adequate sedation in roughly 5 minutes — faster than antipsychotic/benzodiazepine comparators
problem: Sullivan et al. 2020 [6] pooled sedation success (85%) and airway management (20%) and found no significant difference vs controls (sedation RR 1.95, 95% CI 0.47–8.1); it did not report a ~5-minute onset or show ketamine faster than comparators — those data come from individual studies (e.g., Cole 2016 prehospital ketamine vs haloperidol).
whyItMatters: Residents appraising evidence (as the facilitator notes require) are taught a meta-analytic conclusion the paper does not reach and miss its headline safety number (~20% airway management).
evidence: Sullivan N et al., Am J Emerg Med 2020;38(3):655–661, PMID 31902698 abstract: 13 studies; sedation 85%; airway management 20%; comparisons with controls not significant. Cole JB et al., Clin Toxicol 2016 (prehospital ketamine vs haloperidol, median ~5 vs ~17 min).
correction: Meta-analysis of ED/prehospital data shows dissociative-dose ketamine (typically 4–5 mg/kg IM) sedates ~85% of agitated patients, with airway management in ~20% and no statistically significant difference from comparators; individual prehospital studies report onset in roughly 5 minutes, faster than haloperidol

quote: qualitative work shows misses cluster around hypoactive presentations, attribution to dementia or "baseline," and absence of collateral [10]
problem: Schonnop et al. 2022 [10] identified system/attitude themes (varied approaches and infrequent tool use, assessment seen as time-consuming/low priority, unclear responsibility, need for functional understanding), not the clinical phenotype clusters attributed to it.
whyItMatters: Mis-attributes findings; the hypoactive-miss claim is true but rests on other work (e.g., Han 2009), so residents citing [10] would misrepresent it.
evidence: Schonnop R et al., CJEM 2022;24(8):820–831, PMID 36138324 abstract (four themes as listed).
correction: qualitative work attributes misses to inconsistent screening-tool use, assessment perceived as time-consuming and low priority, and unclear ownership of delirium recognition [10]; hypoactive presentations and attribution to dementia or "baseline" are classic miss patterns

quote: large ED cohorts (including Cole et al.) observed no torsades events [5–7]
problem: Citation range [5–7] includes [6], the ketamine meta-analysis, which has nothing on droperidol or torsades.
whyItMatters: Citation identity error; no clinical consequence.
evidence: Reference list: [6] = Sullivan N et al., ketamine meta-analysis.
correction: large ED cohorts (including Cole et al.) observed no torsades events [5,7]

problem: Volume 42 issue 1 of Emerg Med Clin North Am is the 2024 issue (epub 2023); authors are Wolfe C, McCoin N.
evidence: PubMed PMID 37977745: Wolfe C, McCoin N. Emerg Med Clin North Am 42(1):13-29 (epub 2023-07-28; 2024 issue).
verified: PubMed metadata PMID 37977745 / citation lookup matched year 2024
